solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pale pink creeper people bring for arranging around noon (12, two words)

indicators.note: around tells us the rearranged letters wrap round the letter for noon
arranging the letters of people bring puts them into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder taken as written
M is the abbreviation for meridies, noon, as in a.m. and p.m.

explanation.surface: Guests are told to bring a pale pink climbing plant to decorate around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranging' asks for an anagram of PEOPLE BRING, giving BOGPIPERNEL; that goes 'around' M (noon) to give the two-word plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The bog pimpernel is a small creeping plant of wet ground with delicate pale pink flowers.

clue.text: Difficult guy, notice, going in deep

indicators.note: going in says the notice is placed inside the word for deep

parts.note: a bass voice or note is deep
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: A tough character gets a warning and wades into deep water.
explanation.walkthrough: Deep here is the bass voice, not deep water; the notice going in splits it.
explanation.definitionFit: A badass is slang for a tough, aggressive or troublesome person.

clue.text: Parish priest gets playful about describing sermon with bits missing?

indicators.note: about means the word for playful goes round the priest's abbreviation

parts.note: gay in its older sense means merry or playful

explanation.surface: A vicar jokes his way round a sermon that has gaps in it.
explanation.walkthrough: GAY goes 'about' PP. The question mark flags a definition by example: a sermon with bits left out is full of gaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Gappy means full of gaps or breaks, as a patchy, incomplete address would be.

clue.text: Do I stand for the music? Present memory largely faulty

definitions.text: Do I stand for the music?

indicators.note: faulty says the gathered letters are wrong in order and must be rearranged
largely means most of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A concertgoer wonders whether to stand, their recollection of the programme being hazy.
explanation.walkthrough: MEMORY 'largely' is MEMOR; with PR it is shuffled 'faulty'. At the Proms, the London summer concert season, promenaders stand in the arena.
explanation.definitionFit: A prommer is a promenader at the Proms concerts, famous for standing throughout the music.

clue.text: Tote workhouse fare, less grey on top? Stomach turns over it

indicators.note: in a down clue, over it places this piece above the rest
turns means the word for stomach is read backwards

parts.note: tum is a colloquial word for stomach

indicators.note: less signals taking away the grey abbreviation
on top says the removal is from the start of the word

parts.note: gruel was the thin porridge served in workhouses

explanation.surface: Workhouse food without its grey top layer leaves a stomach churning.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutuel is short for pari-mutuel, the pooled betting system known in Britain as the tote.

clue.text: I'm a rep (irregular) getting bonuses only rarely

indicators.note: irregular means the letters come out of order, to be rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A salesman complains that his bonuses come along only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: I'M A REP is rearranged, 'irregular'. 'only rarely' belongs to the definition: the Latin plural is the rarer form beside premiums.
explanation.definitionFit: Premia is an uncommon plural of premium, a bonus or extra payment.

clue.text: Rotor terminal partly reversed — it slows spacecraft

indicators.note: reversed means the chosen letters are read from the end back to the start
partly means only some letters of the two words are used

parts.note: the letters run across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: Part of a rotor's terminal is turned round, and that slows down a spaceship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' takes ORTER from rotOR TERminal, and 'reversed' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A retro is a retrorocket, fired against the direction of travel to brake a spacecraft.

clue.text: Country friend consigned to a bin (improperly put)

indicators.note: improperly put says these letters are placed wrongly and need rearranging

parts.note: ami is French for friend, a common crossword borrowing

explanation.surface: A friend is thrown in the bin, carelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: AMI plus A BIN is 'improperly put', rearranged to give the southern African nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Namibia is a nation in south-west Africa, on the Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Poet's unproductive, open country no longer near

parts.note: a lea is open grassland or meadow
ny is an obsolete spelling of nigh, meaning near

explanation.surface: A poet laments that open land, once close by, now yields nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's' marks the answer as a Spenserian word, and 'no longer' marks NY as an obsolete form.
explanation.definitionFit: Leany is Spenser's word for lean, meaning barren or yielding little.

clue.text: Divorced dad getting into e.g. painting

indicators.note: getting into says the father's word is placed inside the other

parts.note: painting is an example of art
pa is an informal word for dad

explanation.surface: A separated father takes up painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Apart means separated, living away from each other, as a divorced couple are.

clue.text: Author that strangely holds queue up for early books

parts.note: to pen is to write, so a pen stands for the author

indicators.note: holds means the rearranged letters surround the reversed word
strangely says the letters of that are rearranged
in a down clue, up means the word is read bottom to top, so reversed

parts.note: cue is an old spelling of queue, a pigtail

explanation.surface: A writer who oddly makes a queue wait is studying ancient texts.
explanation.walkthrough: THAT strangely becomes TATH, which holds CUE read up the grid (EUC), making TATEUCH; 'queue' as CUE is the old pigtail spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pentateuch is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, the earliest part of scripture.

clue.text: Part of trawler's catch seamen mostly scrapped?

indicators.note: scrapped suggests a scuffle, so the letters are knocked into a new order
mostly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Fishermen fight over part of the haul.
explanation.walkthrough: SEAMEN 'mostly' is SEAME, rearranged; 'scrapped' means fought, not discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A mease is a traditional measure of herrings, around five hundred fish, so a portion of a catch.

clue.text: Decides about sailor with love for bits of bladderwrack

indicators.note: about means the word for decides surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: to settle a matter is to decide it
AB is able seaman, a sailor
love is nil in tennis, so O

explanation.surface: Someone sorts out a sailor and a love affair over some seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: SETTLES goes 'about' AB (able seaman, the crossword sailor) and O, love from tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea bottles are the air-filled bladders of seaweed such as bladderwrack, which keep it afloat.

clue.text: Persona non grata bound to return letter at end of imprisonment

indicators.note: to return means the word for bound is read backwards

parts.note: roped means tied up, bound
the last letter of imprisonment is T, spelt out as the word tee

explanation.surface: An unwelcome visitor, bound and returned, with a letter at the end of his jail term.
explanation.walkthrough: ROPED 'to return' gives DEPOR; the letter T is written as its name, TEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deportee is someone expelled from a country, an unwelcome person sent home.

clue.text: US marine translated cuneiform script

indicators.note: translated suggests changing form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: An American marine deciphers an ancient wedge-shaped script.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumerian, the language of ancient Sumer, was written in cuneiform, the earliest wedge-shaped writing system.

clue.text: I'm held back in a nasty spot — falling foul of one?

definitions.text: I'm held back in a nasty spot — falling foul of one?

indicators.note: in puts the reversed letters inside the word for the spot

parts.note: a stye is an inflamed spot on the eyelid

indicators.note: held back means the letters of I'm are reversed

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in an awkward position grumbles about falling foul of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of I'M are held back to MI, placed in STYE. The whole clue also describes a stymie: being blocked in an awkward spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A stymie is an obstruction or predicament; in golf, a ball blocking another's line to the hole.

clue.text: Silly old fellow person turned away

indicators.note: turned means the word for person is read backwards

parts.note: bod is slang for a person
by can mean aside or away, as in put by

explanation.surface: A foolish old man turns away.
explanation.definitionFit: Dobby is a dialect word for a foolish or doddering old man.

clue.text: Monotonous piece of music? Easy — turn it off

indicators.note: turn and off both suggest the letters are knocked out of order
piece of means just the first letter of the word

parts.note: first letter of music
taken as written

explanation.surface: A listener finds a tune dull and easy listening, and switches it off.
explanation.walkthrough: M, the first 'piece of music', joins EASY, and 'turn it off' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Samey means tediously alike throughout, lacking variety.

clue.text: Chief steward, once? A couple of gypsies holding one up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read bottom to top
holding means the gypsies' word surrounds the letter for one

parts.note: a Rom is a gypsy, so two of them
A can stand for one, as in a single item

explanation.surface: An old-time steward has a pair of gypsies hold someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: ROM ROM 'holding' A gives ROMROAM, which goes 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A maormor was a high steward or regional chief in early Scotland, a historical title.

clue.text: Brave chap has some electric current introduced for this pretty old lamp?

indicators.note: introduced says the unit of current is put inside the other word

parts.note: a lion is a brave person
amp is a unit measuring electric current

explanation.surface: A courageous man brings electricity to a quaint lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A lampion is an old-fashioned small oil lamp, often of coloured glass, used for decoration.

clue.text: Old-style blunderbuss, clumsily repro-ed

indicators.note: clumsily says the letters are handled roughly into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder taken as written, without the hyphen

explanation.surface: An antique gun has been badly reproduced.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedrero was an early gun or small cannon firing stones, akin to a blunderbuss.

clue.text: Stone on rocky road ending in money and fame

indicators.note: ending in places the money letter at the very end of the answer

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the weight

indicators.note: rocky suggests instability, so the letters of road are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder
M is an economics abbreviation for money, as in the M1 and M3 money supply measures

explanation.surface: A rolling stone on the road ends up with money and fame.
explanation.definitionFit: Stardom is the state of being a celebrity, with renown and public attention.

clue.text: Science briefly used to cut open first of songbirds (albeit faultily)

indicators.note: used to cut open says the short form splits the other word and sits inside

parts.note: one is first in counting
sci is a short form of science

explanation.surface: Science is used to dissect songbirds, though not quite perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: SCI is 'used to cut open' ONE. The bracket admits that the group includes crows and others whose song is poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscine relates to the Oscines, the songbird suborder of perching birds, which includes some poor singers.

clue.text: One producing e.g. glühwein, or wallop?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who mulls wine, heating it with spices
second meaning: something that beats heavily

explanation.walkthrough: Wallop is also British slang for beer, so it seems to be a second drink to mull; it is the punch instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A muller is one who mulls drinks, warming and spicing them.

clue.text: More than one sweet spot in Rome at springtime

indicators.note: spot in means the answer can be spotted inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: Several sweet treats are spotted in Rome in spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spot in' finds roME AT Springtime. 'More than one' marks a plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat had an old sense of any food, so sweetmeats are sweets and a meat here is one confection.

clue.text: Dried up parts of big marine inlet repositioned

indicators.note: repositioned says the two parts of the name swap places

parts.note: the Red Sea, a large inlet of the Indian Ocean, in its two parts RED and SEA

explanation.surface: A great sea inlet has dried up, its parts moved around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repositioned' swaps RED and SEA, the two parts of RED SEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Seared means scorched or withered by heat, parched dry.

clue.text: None is gripped by former pestilence receding in capital

indicators.note: is gripped by means the nought is held inside the other word
receding means the word goes backwards

parts.note: lues is an old word for plague or pestilence
O is nothing, zero

explanation.surface: No one is caught by an old plague as it ebbs from a city.
explanation.walkthrough: LUES 'receding' is SEUL, and O 'is gripped by' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Seoul is the capital city of South Korea.

clue.text: Special awards for sea swimmers

parts.note: cups are trophies, awards

explanation.surface: Special trophies are handed out for sea swimmers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sea swimmers' looks like people racing in the sea; it means fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Scups are porgies, food fish of the American Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Tropical plant earl kept in Roman vase

indicators.note: kept in means the letter for earl is put inside the Latin word

parts.note: urna is Latin for an urn or vase

explanation.surface: A lord keeps an exotic plant in a Roman vase.
explanation.definitionFit: Urena is a genus of tropical mallow-family shrubs yielding fibre.

clue.text: Latest bulletin due, apt to be revised

indicators.note: to be revised says the letters must be reworked into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: The newest report is due and is likely to be revised.
explanation.definitionFit: An update is the most recent report bringing news up to date.

clue.text: Inner membranes not left in butchered animal

indicators.note: not shows that the letter for left is excluded from the jumbled letters
butchered suggests cutting up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Some inner tissue is missing from a slaughtered beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' left: take L from ANIMAL to leave ANIMA, which is 'butchered', rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnia, plural of amnion, are the innermost membranes enclosing an embryo.

clue.text: Indian dish, not so hot? Sounds a bit like that — trap of a kind

indicators.note: sounds a bit like says the answer is close in sound to the phrase just given

parts.note: a curry that is cool, said as curry cool

explanation.surface: A curry, not too spicy, gets compared to a kind of carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: A cold curry is a 'curry cool', and the answer 'Sounds a bit like that', a loose match. 'Trap' is a carriage, not a snare.
explanation.definitionFit: A curricle is a light two-wheeled carriage drawn by two horses, and a trap is a small horse-drawn carriage.

clue.text: Low country reclaimed new lines replacing old lager

indicators.note: replacing means the rearranged lines take the place of the word old

parts.note: a polder is low-lying land reclaimed from the sea
the word old, which sits inside the land's name
new signals an anagram, so the letters of lines rearranged to suit the answer

explanation.surface: A low-lying reclaimed land brings in new lines to replace its old lager.
explanation.walkthrough: A polder is reclaimed low-lying land; new lines, replacing the OLD inside it, finish the beer. 'Low country' hints at the Netherlands, but it is the land itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilsener, named after Plzeň in Bohemia, is a pale, light-coloured lager.

clue.text: Henry taken in by five fivers, counterfeit

indicators.note: taken in by means the letter for Henry is placed inside the slang sum

parts.note: a pony is British slang for 25 pounds, five five-pound notes
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Henry is fooled by twenty-five pounds in fake notes.
explanation.walkthrough: H is 'taken in by' PONY, British slang for £25; a fiver is a five-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: Phony means fake or forged, not genuine.

clue.text: Ballerina's dancing — demonstrating this an' all?

definitions.text: Ballerina's dancing — demonstrating this an' all?

indicators.note: dancing says the letters move about into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
the letters to take out of the fodder, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A ballerina dances, showing off this step and everything else besides.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of AN ALL out of BALLERINAS and rearrange the rest, 'dancing'. The whole clue also says a ballerina performs this step.
explanation.definitionFit: A brisé is a ballet step in which the feet beat together in the air.

clue.text: Violinist-poet admitting love for scratchy artwork

parts.note: a scraper is a jocular term for a poor fiddler

indicators.note: admitting means the poet's word lets the nought in

parts.note: a bard is a poet
love is nil in tennis, so O

explanation.surface: A fiddler who is also a poet takes in a lover and some scratched art.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraperboard is a board coated in a dark layer that the artist scratches through to make an image.
